region.en: Cattaraugus Reservation, New York (told by a grandson of Cornplanter)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯保留地（康普蘭特之孫講述）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'Boy rescued by a bear'

summary.en: Left behind by a hunting party that presumes him dead, a missing boy is found by a kind-hearted bear who reasons that her present form would frighten him to death and transforms herself into a woman to adopt him as a playmate for her cubs. He lives in their hollow tree on nuts, corn and berries until fall; the bear explains her device, resumes her proper shape and disappears - and the boy, even grown, was never known to kill a bear.
summary.zh: 獵隊誤以為其已死而離去；瀕死的男孩被仁慈的母熊發現。牠想到現身必會把孩子嚇死，遂化身為女子，攜他回洞與幼熊為伴。男孩與熊家同住空心樹中，以堅果、玉米、莓果為食；秋日獵隊將歸，母熊道破原委，復其原形而隱於林中——男孩此後終生不獵熊。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. In nearly all Iroquois bear-tales the bear figures as a pattern of benevolence.

passages.text: A party of hunters, encamped a long distance from home, discovered, as they were preparing to return, that a young boy of their company was missing. After searching vainly for several days they concluded that he had been killed, and sadly departed without him. They were no sooner gone than the lost child, in an almost famishing condition, was discovered by a very kind-hearted bear, who reasoned thus: 'If I attempt to relieve the child in my present form, he will surely be frightened to death. I will therefore transform myself into a woman and take the boy home with me to become a playmate for my little cubs.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The boy was accordingly rescued from starvation, and, living in the same hollow tree with the bear family, fed with them upon nuts, corn, and berries. But when fall came, and with it the return of the hunters, the good bear explained her device to the boy, saying: 'My cubs must now take care of themselves, and you can rejoin your friends; but always feel kindly toward the bear tribe'; upon which she resumed her proper shape and disappeared into the woods. The boy never, even when grown, was known to kill a bear.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Infant Nursed by Bears and the Monster-Slaying Brothers
title.zh: 熊哺的嬰兒與誅怪兄弟

region.en: Distant hunting camp and the far west (traditional)
region.zh: 遠方的獵營與更西之地（傳統）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'Infant nursed by bears'

summary.en: A famished hunter forces his wife to eat of the bear meat she had killed and hidden until she dies, throws the newborn infant into the hollow tree that held the carcass - and the child is nursed there by a friendly bear. Years later the hunter's son has a mysterious playmate; the father discovers the bear-nursed boy, who cannot understand human speech, and takes home some of his dried-bark bed. The two boys grow strange and strong, go west to kill the great beasts harming the human race, and direct warriors to the carcasses - two of whom die of the stench.
summary.zh: 飢餓的獵人逼妻子吃下她私藏的熊肉，直至其死；又把新生嬰兒丟入曾藏熊屍的空心樹—— friendly bear 在樹中哺育了他。多年後獵人之子有了神秘的玩伴；父親發現熊哺的男孩（不通人語），取其慣用的乾樹皮床回家。兩兄弟漸顯異稟，西行誅殺為害人類的巨獸，命勇士往西尋其屍——有二人因屍臭而斃。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Family violence is at story distance, not depicted for effect.

passages.text: A man and his wife and child went off hunting from an Indian village and encamped a long way from home. At first good luck attended the hunter; at last game became scarce, and day after day he returned empty-handed and famishing. His wife, searching for roots, found a hole in a large tree in which was a black bear, which she succeeded in killing; after cooking some for herself and child she carefully secreted the remainder from her husband. But the boy hid a piece for his father. The hunter was enraged at the conduct of his wife, whom he forced to eat of the meat until she died, with her little infant to which she had given birth the same hour. Then the hunter buried his wife and threw the infant into the hollow tree.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: After this the hunter had better luck, and continued to live in the same place with his little boy. In the course of time he found that his son must have had company, for little foot-prints were to be seen around his wigwam; his son told him that a small boy had been playing with him. The next day the father watched and saw a little boy leave the tree where he had placed what he supposed to be the dead child. 'You are my child,' he said; but the boy could not understand him, and ran away to the tree, where the hunter discovered he had been nourished and cared for by a friendly bear. The hunter would not kill the kind benefactor, but took some of the soft bed of dried bark to his home, whereupon the child was happy and contented to remain with his father and brother.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: In time the two excelled in hunting and brought home owls and strange birds. Finally they told their father they were going to the far west to kill the great beasts which were harming the human race. The hunter, who perceived that the children were becoming very strange, was afraid of them and consented. They bade him get three of the bravest warriors to follow them to the west, where they would find the carcasses of the animals which they would kill; the warriors found the traces of the boys and in time the carcasses almost reduced to bones - and two of the men died of the stench.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Man and His Step-Son: The Porcupine Hole and the Bear Family
title.zh: 人與繼子：豪豬穴與熊家

region.en: Porcupine hole in the deep woods (told by a granddaughter of Brant)
region.zh: 深林中的豪豬穴（布蘭特之孫女講述）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The man and his step-son'

summary.en: A hated step-son is lured into a porcupine's hole and sealed in. An old woman below calls an animal council - the fox's geese are no good raw, the deer's browse unsuitable - and the bear's nuts win; the boy lives years with bear cubs until a dog brings the hunter to chop the tree, killing the old bear and cubs. Mistaking the boy's cub-cry for another cub, the hunter tames him, teaches him speech, and marries him to his daughter; his mother-in-law's taunts about tender bear-meat drive him to kill a bear, and on his return he falls on a sharp stick and dies.
summary.zh: 被憎恨的繼子被誘入豪豬穴封死。洞下的老婦召集獸議——狐之鵝禽生食不宜，鹿之草料難以下嚥——熊的堅果獲選；男孩與幼熊同住多年，直至獵犬引獵人砍樹，老熊與幼熊俱斃。獵人誤將男孩的幼熊啼聲當作另一幼崽，馴之教語，並以女妻之；岳母屢嘲他不獵嫩熊肉，他終殺一熊，歸途中跌於尖枝而死。

passages.text: A certain man had a step-son whom he hated. He saw a porcupine's hole one day while hunting. 'See here,' he said at home, 'I have found a porcupine's nest. I want you to creep into the hole and catch some of the young ones. Come, crawl in.' The boy obeyed, and as soon as his heels were in, the step-father closed up the hole and made him a prisoner. When he had found himself betrayed he cried and cried till he cried himself asleep. When he awakened he found that he was in a room, and an old woman brought him something to eat, so bitter that he refused it. She called many animals around her to a council - wolves, bears, foxes, and deer - and asked what they would advise to give which might support a human being. The fox said, 'I live on geese and fowls. I'll take him, but still he can't eat raw food.' The deer and each animal in turn told what they lived upon, but none could offer proper food for a lad. Last of all the bear spoke: 'I live on nuts, and he can live with my young ones.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: So this was agreed to, and the boy was given over to the keeping of the bear, who kept him for several years. One day the bear said, 'A hunter is coming; he means to chop down the tree.' True enough, next day a dog ran barking up, and the tree was cut down and the old bear and two cubs were killed. The hunter thought there might be still another cub, so he looked into the tree; the boy made a noise just like the cubs. The hunter caught him, and was so astonished at his appearance that, instead of killing him, he took him to his wigwam, tamed him, and taught him to speak and to grow up like a man.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: After some years he forgot he had lived like a bear. He married a daughter of the hunter, but his mother-in-law was always angry because he never brought home tender bear-meat. So at last he went hunting and killed a bear, but on his return home he fell on a sharp stick and was instantly killed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Boy and His Grandmother: The Four-Faced Head in the Lake
title.zh: 男孩與祖母：湖中四面之首

region.en: Lake in the western woods (forbidden direction), Seneca country
region.zh: 塞內卡之地西方禁行的湖

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The boy and his grandmother'

summary.en: Forbidden to go west, the boy disobeys and meets a disembodied voice that threatens hurricanes and hail-spears against his grandmother's cabin; he laughs each threat away, turning the cabin into a rock - and, cheated of his ice-spears, resolves to punish the 'old fellow.' With a stone-charm around his neck he finds a great head with a face on every side in the middle of the lake, hurls the stone (which grows huge as it flies) into the water; the lake dries, the animals die, and the wizard remains only as a large frog, which the boy kills - and no more trouble ever came to him or his grandmother.
summary.zh: 男孩違禁西行，遇見一個無形之聲：先以颶風、再以冰矛相脅。他一一笑納——把小屋化作岩石，反將冰矛視為漁叉之喜（卻尋不見）。為懲罰這「老傢伙」，他頸掛石符，至湖心見一四面有臉的巨首；擲石入湖，石飛愈大，湖水沸騰。次日湖涸獸斃，巫者只餘一隻大蛙，男孩殺之——從此他與祖母再無煩擾。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. The four-faced lake-head is a distinct water-monster type.

passages.text: An old woman lived with her grandson in the wilderness. 'Never, my grandson, never go west - go always to the east,' she would say; but he questioned how and why, and thought to himself that on the first opportunity he would see for himself. As he neared the lake he heard the man's voice: 'Ah! ah! my little fellow, I see you... What would you think if I sent a hurricane to tear your grandmother's cabin all up?' 'Oh, I should like it. We have hard work to get wood.' 'You had better run home and see.' As he neared his cabin the hurricane was upon them, but the boy only laughed and said, 'We will throw the house into a rock' - and he turned it into a rock, and when the hurricane was over they were unharmed, and found plenty of wood to burn.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Again the voice threatened a great hailstorm with spears as sharp as needles. 'I have always wanted some spears; I would be glad of some... I need spears for fishing; let them come.' The house was turned to rock again, and when the storm ended the ground was covered with spears - but when he brought the pole he could not find any. 'They are melted - they were ice,' said his grandmother. The boy mourned aloud, 'What can I do to punish the old fellow?'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Taking with him a stone round his neck as a charm, he started off once more, and all at once saw in the middle of the lake a great head, with a face on every side of it. He cried out, 'Ha! ha! uncle, I have you now. How should you like it if the lake dried up?' 'That it will never do,' said the voice. 'Go home,' mocked the lad, 'and see!' And he threw the stone which he had: as it whirled through the air it became very large and fell into the lake, when, at once, the water began to boil. Next morning he went over to the lake and found it all dried up and all the animals dead, and only a large frog remained, into which the man had been turned. So the boy killed the frog, and no more trouble ever came to him or his grandmother.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Dead Hunter: Night in the Corpse Wigwam

region.en: Empty wigwam on the far hunting trail

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The dead hunter'

summary.en: A hunting couple shelters overnight in a wigwam where a dead man lies laid out with his tomahawk and fine things. At midnight the corpse sits up and eats their bread; the hunter sends his wife for water, pinches the baby to follow her, and flees - the dead man coming behind with a lighted torch. He escapes into a hollow log under the dead man's hatchet-strokes until the hatchet breaks: 'I must go; my night is coming on.' The chief afterwards burns the dead man's wigwam to ashes.
summary.zh: 獵人夫婦夜宿一間停放死者的屋中。半夜屍者坐起吞食他們的麵包；獵人支妻去取水，捏哭嬰兒藉口跟隨，倉皇而逃——死人持火炬緊追不捨。獵人鑽入空心圓木，忍受死者斧擊，直至斧柄斷裂：「我該走了，我的夜晚要到了。」事後酋長命人把死人屋焚為灰燼。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Companion piece to Cusick's ghost-house and its burial reform.

passages.text: A man and his wife went hunting, and after a hard day's march came to an empty wigwam and found in it a dead man, laid out with his tomahawk and all his fine things. They found corn in plenty, made bread, and went to bed, the man on one side and the woman and her baby on the other, placing some of the bread between them. In the middle of the night they heard a noise, and the dead man was sitting up and eating.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: 'We are all dead folks,' cried the hunter, 'if we remain here'; so he made a pretense, and whispered to the squaw, 'You must go for water. I will mind the child.' As soon as she was gone he pinched the baby till it cried. 'I must follow the mother or the child will die.' He hastened and soon caught up with the woman, but behind him came the dead man, holding a lighted torch. To save themselves they put the child down on the ground, and the hunter hurried his wife on faster and faster, but the sound of steps behind them was plainer and plainer. So the man let his wife go, and fled on by himself as hard as he could.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Soon he came to a hollow log, into which he crept. The steps came nearer and nearer, until at last he felt the strokes of the dead man's hatchet, and heard the dead man's voice saying, 'Ah! you are here. I have caught you.' Then the dead man took a pole and tried to poke the hunter out of the hollow, but he could not; at last his hatchet broke, and then the hunter heard him say, 'I must go; my night is coming on.' After a while the hunter crept out of the hollow log and went after his wife and child, and returned to the settlement and told all about it; and the chief sent and burnt up the dead man's wigwam until it was nothing but ashes.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: A Hunter's Adventures: Geese-Borne, Stump-Jailed, and Flying Home
title.zh: 獵人歷險：雁載、困樁與飛行歸鄉

region.en: Lake and southern hunting grounds, Seneca Reservation
region.zh: 塞內卡保留地的湖泊與南方獵場

texts.period: Told by Mr. Snow, Seneca Reservation (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'A hunter's adventures'

summary.en: Out of arrows, a hunter ties geese to his belt with basswood withes from below the flock and is carried into the air; unfastening them for a gradual descent, he falls into a tall hollow stump and is imprisoned nearly two days until women wood-choppers - frightened by his cries - fetch aid. Resupplied, he hunts far south, preserves the oil of deer and bear in leathern bottles, makes himself thin deerskin wings, and flies home, dropping bottles to the women who rescued him - who to this day do not know from whence they came.
summary.zh: 箭矢用盡的獵人以椴皮繩自雁群之下縛雁於腰，被拖上天空；鬆綁徐降之際全體掙脫，他墜入高大的空心樹樁，受困近兩日，直至伐木的婦人們聞其呼救驚懼求助。補給再足後南狩，把鹿熊之油藏於皮囊；再以薄鹿皮製翼飛行歸鄉，途中將油瓶拋給恩人——至今她們仍不知油瓶從何而來。

passages.text: A hunter far from home had expended all of his arrows when he arrived at a lake and saw a great number of wild geese. He procured a quantity of second-growth bass-wood bark, which he tore into withes; these he fastened to his belt, then, swimming out into the lake, he dove down under the floating flock and succeeded in tying a few of the geese to his belt, whereupon the struggling geese, with their companions, flew up into the air, carrying the hunter with them. While unfastening a few of the tied ones, so that he might be let down to the ground in a gradual manner, the whole of the captured ones broke away, and the poor hunter fell into a tall and hollow stump, from which he found it impossible to free himself.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: He remained in this miserable prison nearly two days, when he with joy heard a thumping sound upon the outside of the stump, and also the voices of women choppers who were cutting down the stump for wood; but the cries of the man on the inside frightened the women so much that they went away in search of aid. The hunter was finally delivered safely from his perilous situation, and he remained with his kind rescuers until he had again provided himself with a large stock of arrows.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: He started anew for a hunt farther to the south, built a lodge, and had excellent luck in killing large numbers of deer, bears, and other game, the oil of which he carefully preserved in leathern bottles. When he concluded to return home he remembered his experience in flying, so he prepared wings for himself, made from thinly-dressed deer-skin. Taking his bottles of oil for ballast, he started homeward; as he passed over the lodges of the good women who had rescued him, he threw down several bottles to these his good friends, who to this day do not know from whence they came. After this the flying hunter flew swiftly and safely to his home, and all assembled to listen to the hunter's narration of his exploits and adventures.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Old Man's Lessons to His Nephew: Bear Marks and Feast Sticks
title.zh: 老人對姪兒的教導：熊蹤與宴籤

region.en: Solitary lodge in the Seneca woods

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The old man's lessons to his nephew'

summary.en: An uncle teaches bear-hunting by hint: 'shoot just where there is no hair' - and the nephew shoots his uncle's finger, then his pursed lips, while the bear makes off; a second lesson ends with the bear walking out through the fallen corn-stalks; and the feast-stick errand finds the boy literally inviting 'the tall tree' and 'the swamp' to dinner. Tired of his uncle's parables, the young fellow goes off into the world to learn his lessons by experience - a Seneca cousin-tale to Parker's Boy Who Could Not Understand.
summary.zh: 叔父以暗示教獵：「射沒有毛的地方」——姪兒便射中叔父的手指，又射穿其努起的嘴唇，眼睜睜看著熊逃走；第二次課上，玉米稈全倒在熊面前，牠大搖大擺出洞。最後的宴籠任務裡，男孩把「高樹」與「沼澤」請來赴宴。厭倦了叔父的謎語課，少年便出外向世界學習——此即帕克《聽不懂的男孩》的塞內卡近親故事。

passages.text: One day as the young man was out he saw a hole in a tree, and the claw marks of the bear showing that he had gone up; in the morning they started together. 'Our plan is to knock around the outside of the tree and make the bear uneasy; presently he will come out... If you will shoot just where there is no hair, you will surely kill him.' The young man saw that the paws were without hair and he hit the bear on the fore-paw. 'Shoot again,' said the uncle. So he shot the other paw. Then the old man pointed and said, 'Shoot here.' And the nephew aimed and shot the point of his uncle's finger. Then the old man's hand hurt him, so to direct his nephew he pursed out his lips and pointed with them, and the young man shot through his lips. Then the bear came down and made his way off, while the uncle was explaining that his meaning had been to shoot under the fore legs. The young man asked, 'Why did you not say so?'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The next day the young man found a large bear in a hole near the root of a tree; the uncle went into the corn field, gathered the corn-stalks and stuck them around the entrance to the hole, then knocked on the other side of the tree - and the bear came out, as, of course, there was no reason why he should not, for the stalks fell before him. The young man took his arms and went home. 'You did not understand,' said the old man. 'You should have shot him as he left the den; first on one side then on the other.' 'After this,' expostulated the young man, 'make your explanations clearer and do not give so many illustrations.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: One day the old man said, 'I'm going to make a feast. You can invite the guests. I cut sticks to represent so many friends. Go to the highest tree you can find and leave this stick there. Then go along till you find a place all swamp - bad place, and leave one stick there.' So the nephew went around and used up the sticks and returned. Yet when the day came and the feast was ready, nobody came. 'How,' inquired the young man, 'could the tall tree and the swamp come here?' So they ate together, and then the young fellow went off in the world to learn his lessons by experience, for he had become tired of his uncle's parables.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: Hemlock Bows: The Faithless Wife and the Man in the Black-Ash Tree
title.zh: 鐵杉弓：不貞之妻與黑梣樹中人

region.en: Black-ash tree by the hunting cabin, Seneca country
region.zh: 塞內卡獵屋旁的黑梣樹

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The hunter and his faithless wife'

summary.en: Hemlock Bows, who can shake thirty deer small as squirrels and back again, follows his truant wife to a hollow black-ash tree where a fine man in a feathered turban comes out to meet her; his arrow passes between them and she beats him blind, turns the children into the snow and burns the cabin. The dog houses the children; a bear carries off the little girl; the boy survives being swallowed by a great fish, is cut out alive by two fisher women, and later shoots the eagle at his mother's wedding games, rescues father, sister and dog, and burns the cabin where his mother dies - from whose ashes rises a screech owl.
summary.zh: 能將三十隻鹿搖小如松鼠再搖回原大的「鐵杉弓」，跟蹤不貞的妻子至一棵中空的黑梣樹，一位戴羽冠的俊美男子自樹中出迎。他的箭從二人之間穿過，反遭妻子打瞎，孩子被棄雪中，屋亦被焚。犬為孩子搭雪屋；幼女被熊叼走；男孩被大魚吞下卻活著被兩位捕魚婦女剖出。他後來在母親改嫁的射鷹競賽中射中鷹，救出父親、妹妹與犬，焚燒母親所在的屋——母親死後，灰燼中鑽出一隻啼叫的鴞。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Marital violence is story-register, not endorsement.

passages.text: There was a man whose name was Hemlock Bows; he would kill so many deer that he could not carry them all home - he took them and shook them, and shook, till they were as small as squirrels, and carried them all home, and when he got there he shook, and shook, till they were good-sized deer again. After the birth of her second child the wife seemed to care no more for her husband: when he went hunting she would wash and dress up very fine, take a long strap and an ax, and leave the children alone all day. The little boy told his father all about his mother going away every day, and he resolved to follow her. He tracked her very closely to a large black-ash tree, which was hollow; a very nice-looking man came out of the tree to meet her, wearing a turban filled with bright feathers. When the man kissed her the hunter drew his bow and shot, and the arrow went between him and the woman. She was very angry, took a club and beat her husband till he could not see; then she went home, put the boy and girl out in the cold and snow, set fire to the cabin, and went off.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The dog fixed the boy and girl in a house in the snow, and the next day they started on a long walk. While the boy was traveling with his little sister on his back she saw a flock of large white turkeys and wanted one; while he was after it a bear came and carried off the little girl, and the dog followed after the bear. The boy cried and cried, wished that he might die; he tried to hang himself, but the strap broke; he jumped down a steep place onto a lot of stones, but still he was unhurt. He plunged into a lake, but it was very shallow, and soon a great fish came towards him with its great mouth wide open. Not far off lived a woman and her daughter who had fences of osier fixed in the lake to catch fish; in the morning they killed and dressed a very large one, and when they cut it up there they found the boy alive.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: They heard that the boy's mother was going to be married to another man. Between two cabins was a long stick put up, and on it was an eagle, and the one that shot the eagle was to marry the woman. The boy went among the wigwams and found his sister hanging to a crane in a chimney, and near her the dog; he got his father, sister, and dog away, then went back and set fire to the cabin his mother was in; it burned so fast that she could not get out, and she died. When her head cracked open it shook the ground, and out of the ashes of his mother there rose up a screech owl. His father got well, and they all went to live with the woman and her daughter - the old man married the woman, and the boy the daughter, and so they were happy at last.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Charmed Suit: The Impostor with the Birds That Would Not Light His Pipe
title.zh: 魔法衣：鳥兒不為其點菸的冒名者

region.en: Chief's village to the west of the solitary lodge

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The charmed suit'

summary.en: Raised quietly in a solitary lodge, a boy is sent daily to listen until he hears a woman's song naming him: 'I belong to the wolf clan. I am going to marry him.' His uncle dresses him in magic finery - a swan that comes alive on his head, a pipe lit by two little birds, spittle that becomes wampum - but warns of a man at a stream who will beg help killing wild cats. The youth stays the night; the tempter covers him with prickly bark, steals his charmed suit and goes to the chief's daughters, who are deceived except the younger sister. Found in a field asleep, the true youth dreams a dream before a great council: the birds fill his pipe, the swan comes alive, his spittle becomes wampum - and the impostor is left in his own rags.
summary.zh: 孤屋長大的少年日日聽聲，直至聽見女聲唱出：「我屬狼氏族，我將嫁給他。」叔父為他備下魔法行頭——會復活的天鵝冠、由兩隻小鳥點火的菸斗、唾沫化貝珠——並警告途中會有人藉殺野貓求援。少年留宿被騙，被荊皮所蟄，行頭盡失；冒名者前往酋長二女處，只有妹妹識破。真少年在田中被妹妹發現，遂於大議會上「作夢」：鳥兒為他點菸、天鵝復活、唾沫成珠——冒名者被打回原形的破衣。

passages.text: An old man brought up his son very quietly in a solitary place, sending him daily into the woods to listen. Morning after morning he heard snow-birds, wolves, owls; at last, as the sun began to rise, he heard quite a new sound, like a voice singing: 'Ha-hum-weh, Ha-hum-weh, Wa-he-dum-nae, Sru-gua he' - 'I belong to the wolf clan. I am going to marry him.' It was a sweet woman's voice. 'The chief of a distant village sends his two daughters to see us,' said the father. He threw ashes all over the boy's bed and put on him his best feathers: 'Do not look at the maidens when they come in; they come to see me, not you; hold your head down while they stay.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The sisters refused to sit by the old man, cleared up the wigwam, and when the boy went to sleep they lifted him out of his dirty bed strewn with ashes and put him into their clean bed. In the morning the younger one admired him: 'What a beautiful young man!' The old man said, 'Good woman; can clean up, can cook, can make good wife,' and gave his son magic arrows for luck in hunting, and dressed him with a swan stuffed: 'when you take this outside it will be on your head, but it will soon come back to life... many deer and bears will follow your track.' He warned of dangers in the path: 'There stands a man and he will try to kill you. He will call out to you that he has a couple of wild cats... Pay no attention.' And he hung up a curious thing of colored string and deep red elk hair: if it came down almost to the ground, his nephew was in danger.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: At the stream the stranger begged for help against the wild cats, then asked him to stop all night. The uncle at home watched the signal go down almost to the ground and cried out in alarm - but the youth agreed to stay. The old man gathered sharp prickly bark, pretending it gave a good light, placed it on the sleeping youth, who writhed in agony; then he took off the young man's handsome clothes, dressed him in his own old rags, and started off to the chief's house with the pipe whose two little birds lighted it, the spotted deer skin, and the handsome bag. The younger sister was disappointed - 'This cannot be the young man' - and observed that the bag did not obey the stranger's command to stand up, and that the birds would not light his pipe 'for a stranger.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Husking corn in the fields one day, the younger sister found a man asleep near a fire, and recognized the beautiful young man, how greatly changed! She brought him food, and he said, 'I will make a dream. Go and tell the chief, your father, that I have dreamed a dream and all the people must come to hear it.' At the great council he told his story in the form of a dream, and when he spoke of the birds they came and filled his pipe, and the swan skin when placed upon his head also came to life, and his spittle became wampum. So the chief knew he was the rightful owner of the clothes and they were returned to him, and the impostor was obliged to resume his old rags. The young man was then married to the faithful maiden, and became in time a noted chief.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Lad and the Chestnuts: The White Heron's Watch
title.zh: 少年與栗子：白鷺的守望

region.en: Great river and the guarded chestnut tree beyond (traditional)
region.zh: 大河與彼岸受守的栗樹（傳統）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The lad and the chestnuts'

summary.en: A younger brother secretly watches his elder cook half a chestnut in a magic kettle that grows with every whip-stroke; the lad's excess fills the house, and the brother, declaring he must die, wastes away singing 'Bring me my pipe and let me die.' Beyond an almost uncrossable river stands the ancestral chestnut tree, watched day and night by a white heron set by half a dozen women who come out with war-clubs at his Thr-hr-hr. The lad crosses on a canoe of three inches drawn large, bribes the heron with the seeds of a plant he dearly likes, fills his bag, cuts five fish-lines thrown by the women, and returns in time to cook the chestnuts and restore his brother.
summary.zh: 弟弟偷看兄長以魔法釜煮半顆栗子——鞭一下釜便大一圈；弟弟學樣，釜大漲滿屋。兄長哀歌「把菸斗拿來，讓我死吧」。在幾不可渡的大河彼岸，立著祖傳的栗樹，由六位婦女所設的白鷺日夜守望，一有聲響便發出Thr-hr-hr的警號，眾婦持棒而出。弟弟以三寸小舟抽大渡河，以鷺所嗜的豆狀草籽引開牠，裝滿栗袋，連斷五根魚線而歸，及時煮熟栗子救回兄長。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Second version of the chestnut cycle Parker also records.

passages.text: At daylight the elder set off to hunt. Cautiously the boy lifted the trap-door, and there he at once saw the kettle. In it lay half a chestnut. As night drew on he took the kettle, scraped up the chestnut, put in some water, and found the stick. He at once commenced whipping the kettle as he had seen his brother do, saying, 'Now my kettle will grow large' - and it did; but it kept on growing larger and larger, to his surprise, until it filled the whole room, and he had to go up on the roof to stir it from the outside. When the elder brother returned he said, 'What are you doing?' 'I found the kettle,' replied the younger, 'and was getting your supper.' 'Woe is me,' said the elder, 'now I must die.' He struck and struck the kettle, and reduced it by every blow, until at last he could restore it to its place.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Day by day he grew weaker, and after each smoke sang, 'Hah geh-he geh, Non ta ge je o dah!' - 'Bring me my pipe and let me die.' At length the brother said, 'Far, far away is a large river, which it is almost impossible to cross. On the further side stands a house; near it is a tree, a chestnut tree; there my forefathers gathered chestnuts long ago, but now none can reach it, for there stands night and day a white heron watching the tree... He is set there by the women folks; half a dozen of them take care of him, and for them he watches. If he hears a sound he makes his Thr-hr-hr. Then the women come out with war-clubs... Even a mouse is suspected of being a man. There is no chance, no chance at all.' But the brother said, 'I must go and try this for your sake; I cannot have you die.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: He departed after making a little canoe about three inches long; at the river he drew it out and out until it was a good size, and in it he crossed, then made it small again and put it in his pouch. He called a mole out of the ground, which sniffed around a little plant, the seed of which the heron dearly likes - like a bean. Following the mole under the leaves until he neared the heron, he threw the seeds to the bird, and whilst it was occupied and noticed nothing else, the boy filled his bag with chestnuts and set off homewards. The heron gave his warning Thr-hr-hr, but the lad was already far away. Once more he took out his canoe, and was on the water when the women rushed out: they threw a long fish line and caught his canoe, but he cut it and got loose - and so on till they had no lines left. He reached home and shouted, 'Now, brother, I'm home with the chestnuts, will you have your pipe?' And the brother said, 'You have done me a great favor, now I shall be well, and we will be happy.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.
